Curing HIV with gene editing

By: Eugene Botha | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Gene therapy snips HIV out of infected cells and makes uninfected cells resistant

Summary:
For the first time, researchers have used a gene-editing technique already used to produce cells resistant to HIV infection to target HIV-infected cells. They have managed to remove HIV genes completely from infected cells, as shown by reductions in the cells' overall rate of HIV production. In cells not already infected, the therapy has itself become part of their genome, producing cells that are resistant to infection for a prolonged period.

Further information:
HIV Genes Have Been Cut Out of Live Animals Using CRISPR. This research will make it more possible to one day do the same in humans

In a first, scientists led by Kamel Khalili, director of the Comprehensive NeuroAIDS Center at Temple University, report in the journal Gene Therapy that they have for the first time successfully eliminated HIV genes from the genomes of mice and rats infected with the virus.

While rodents don’t get infected with HIV in the same way that humans do, Khalili and his team engineered the animals to incorporate specific HIV genes into nearly every cell in their body, from the brain, heart, liver, kidney lungs and spleen to their blood cells. They then created a pair of molecular scissors using a gene editing technique called CRISPR to snip out the viral genes. CRISPR’s power lies in the fact that it’s precise enough to find and cut out just the viral genes, leaving the animals’ own DNA intact.

In previous studies, Khalili used CRISPR to snip out HIV from cells taken from HIV positive people and grown in a lab dish. But proving that it works in a living animal is a huge step forward to developing the technique as a possible treatment, or even cure, for HIV-AIDS.

In the study, Khalili studied CRISPR’s ability to remove HIV from both mice and rat models, and found that overall, it was successful in cutting out the virus in more than 50% of the cells of each type. Surprisingly, he achieved this with two simple injections of the molecular CRISPR scissors into a vein in the animals’ tails. “It’s very simple,” he says. “If this technology gets into the clinic to treat human patients, it’s not going to be very complicated. You don’t have to bring the patient to the clinic and do a bone marrow transplant or all kinds of complicated technology. You can basically apply this to any setting.”

That’s important is this technique eventually becomes a way to treat people infected with HIV, since the bulk of them live in developed countries where health care facilities aren’t always available.

Khalili says this is only one step, albeit an important one, toward that goal. He is currently conducting more studies to determine what dose and how often the CRISPR needs to be given, and monitoring for any side effects of the treatment as well. Because the CRISPR molecule targets HIV genes, it’s unlikely that they will have adverse effects on human DNA, but that’s still an unanswered question that doctors and regulators like the Food and Drug Administration will need to know before they allow the strategy to be tested in human patients.

Still, if it’s possible to eliminated HIV from people who are infected, that could lead the way toward curing people of the disease. While anti-HIV drugs are very effective in lowering levels of the virus, they still can’t ferret out every last virus hiding, latent, in some cells. Those hidden reservoirs of HIV are the most dangerous — they can reactivate and cause disease years after the initial infection. But if CRISPR can eliminate them, then that would essentially cure people of their infection. “The first step is to permanently inactivate those viruses incorporated in cells,” says Khalili. “If we can do that, and reach that level, then we may be able to functionally cure individuals or have a sterilizing cure.”

Researchers from Lewis Katz School of Medicine at Temple University Successfully Excise HIV DNA from Animals
POSTED ON MAY 18, 2016
Using gene editing technology, researchers at the Lewis Katz School of Medicine at Temple University have, for the first time, successfully excised a segment of HIV-1 DNA – the virus responsible for AIDS – from the genomes of living animals. The breakthrough, described online this month in the journal Gene Therapy, is a critical step in the development of a potentially curative strategy for HIV infection.

“In a proof-of-concept study, we show that our gene editing technology can be effectively delivered to many organs of two small animal models and excise large fragments of viral DNA from the host cell genome,” explained lead investigator on the study, Kamel Khalili, PhD, Laura H. Carnell Professor and Chair of the Department of Neuroscience, Director of the Center for Neurovirology, and Director of the Comprehensive NeuroAIDS Center at the Lewis Katz School of Medicine at Temple University (LKSOM).

Current treatment for HIV infection is centered on the use of a combination of antiretroviral drugs. While antiretroviral drug therapy can effectively suppress HIV replication, it has no ability to eliminate HIV-1 from infected cells. Moreover, when antiretroviral therapy is interrupted, HIV replication rebounds, placing patients at risk for developing acquired immune deficiency syndrome, or AIDS. Such latent infections develop because HIV DNA is able to persist in the genomes of CD4+ memory T-cells and perhaps in other cellular reservoirs where the virus remains silent and is unaffected by current therapy.

In earlier research, Dr. Khalili and colleagues were able to show that their novel gene editing system, which is based on CRISPR/Cas9 technology, has the extraordinary ability to eliminate HIV-1 from infected cells in vitro with no adverse effect on the host cells. In ex vivo experiments using clinical specimens, including T-cells from patients infected with HIV that were expanded in culture, they showed that viral replication was significantly reduced following treatment with the gene editing system.

The latest study was designed specifically to test whether the gene editing technology could also eliminate HIV-1 in transgenic rats and mice, in which HIV DNA is incorporated into the genome of every cell and organ of the experimental animals. In order to deliver the technology to cells in living animals, Dr. Khalili and colleagues employed a recombinant adeno-associated viral (rAAV) vector delivery system. They also engineered the gene editing apparatus to cleave the integrated HIV-1 DNA in the host cell genome, leading to excision of the viral DNA fragment from the host genome.

Two weeks after delivery of the rAAV CRISPR/Cas-9 molecules into the bloodstream, the researchers analyzed the DNA of tissues collected from the animals. The results showed that the targeted segment of HIV-1 DNA had been excised from the viral genome in every tissue, including the brain, heart, kidney, liver, lungs, spleen, and blood cells. Analyses of viral RNA in the rat model showed that the strategy significantly reduced levels of HIV-1 RNA in circulating lymphocytes, as well as in lymph nodes, indicating that viral genome excision had significantly impacted HIV-1 gene expression in cells carrying integrated viral DNA.

“The ability of the rAAV delivery system to enter many organs containing the HIV-1 genome and edit the viral DNA is an important indication that this strategy can also overcome viral reactivation from latently infected cells and potentially serve as a curative approach for patients with HIV,” said Dr. Khalili. The excision strategy used in this study, which led to the removal of a large fragment of HIV-1 DNA, eliminates any chance for the development of replication-competent virus or escape events.

The clinical implications of the new study are far-reaching. The gene editing platform by itself may be able to eradicate HIV-1 DNA from patients, but it is also highly flexible and potentially could be used in combination with existing antiretroviral drugs to further suppress viral RNA. It also could be adapted to target mutated strains of HIV-1.

Dr. Khalili noted that a clinical trial could happen within the next several years. In the meantime, the next step is to conduct a follow-up study in a larger group of animals, in which the researchers plan to monitor for effects of the treatment, its safety, and other important indices.

Other researchers contributing to the study include Rafal Kaminski, Chaoran Yin, Jessica Otte, Jennifer Gordon, and Wenhui Hu, Department of Neuroscience, Center for Neurovirology, Lewis Katz School of Medicine at Temple University; Ramona Bella and Pasquale Ferrante, Microbiology and Clinical Microbiology, Department of Biomedical, Surgical and Dental Sciences, University of Milan, Milan, Italy; Howard E. Gendelman, Department of Pharmacology and Experimental Neuroscience, University of Nebraska Medical Center; and Hailong Li and Rosemarie Booze, Behavioral Neuroscience, Department of Psychology, University of South Carolina.

The research was supported in part by grants provided by the National Institutes of Health (P30MH092177 and R01NS087971).

Editor’s Note: Drs. Khalili, Hu, and Kaminski are named inventors on patents that cover the viral gene editing technology that is the subject of this published journal article. In addition to the foregoing interests, Kamel Khalili, is a co-founder, board member, scientific advisor, and holds equity in Excision Biotherapeutics, a biotech start-up which has licensed the viral gene editing technology from Temple University for commercial development and clinical trials. Jennifer Gordon serves as an unpaid scientific advisor to Excision Biotherapeutics. The option to license the viral gene editing technology was signed prior to the acceptance of this manuscript. The authors declare that this work was produced solely by the authors and that no other individuals or entities influenced any aspects of the work including, but not limited to, the study conception and design; data acquisition, analysis and interpretation; and writing of the manuscript. The work was funded by the National Institutes of Health. No other entities provided funds for the work. The authors further declare that they have received no financial compensation from any other third parties for any aspects of the published work.

Press Release:


CRISPR HIV Cure?
US scientists have made world headlines by looking at HIV and Aids as a genetic disease, rather than an infectious one. A remarkable gene-editing tool called CRISPR creates veritable ‘genetic scissors’, cutting DNA to remove all traces of the HI virus in cells. Carte Blanche asks: Is there a cure for HIV on the horizon?


Script:


Prof Kamel Khalili:
If the virus is causing the disease the only way that you can cure the disease associated with virus is eliminating the virus
V/O:
Prof Kamel Khalili is a neuroscientist at Temple University in Philadelphia in the US. His department has pioneered a new way to tackle HIV, offering a possible cure for this global epidemic.
Khalili:
About 70 Million people got infected worldwide with HIV and half of them die.
V/O:
South Africa has the biggest and most high profile HIV epidemic in the world. More than 6 million people, 12% of the population, are infected with HIV. About 40 percent of these people receive antiretroviral treatment.
LINK:
And HIV and Aids continue to exact a grim toll on the South African population claiming about a hundred and eighty thousand lives annually.
V/O:
And the economic cost is staggering.
Michael Pepper:
It is a major problem and it does occupy a lot of time and resources in our public health setting with an annual expenditure of approximately 20 billion rand.
V/O:
Prof Michael Pepper is the Director of the Institute for Cellular and Molecular Medicine at the University of Pretoria and says treating HIV is so difficult because of the nature of the virus.
Devi:
So talk me through the process of how HIV infection happens.
Pepper:
HIV docks onto the surface of the target cell, say for example a T-cell. Once it is docked onto the surface it ejects its contents into the cell.
V/O:
This content injected into the cell contains genetic material and can combine with the DNA in the host cell.
Michael Pepper:
And that DNA is then integrated into the host DNA. So the host DNA carries the virus in the form of DNA in that cell that has now been infected.
V/O:
The HI virus mainly infects cells associated with the human immune system such as T-cells.
Devi:
So, HIV is imprinted then in your DNA?
Pepper:
It constitutes part of your DNA, yes, absolutely.
Khalili:
And then the cell becomes a factory for the viral production continuously making HIV and budding out from the cells and take the neighbouring cells and that’s the way that basically infection goes on.
V/O:
As the infection builds, the body’s immune system becomes compromised and people become vulnerable to lethal infections and cancers.
LINK:
The disease is kept under control by the use of ARV’s or anti-retroviral drugs.
V/O:
But Kamel says this is not the ultimate solution.
Khalili:
The current anti-retroviral therapy, which is a useful treatment of AIDS does not eliminate the virus. What is does is inhibits, suppresses replication of the virus.
V/O:
But even if the virus is not multiplying in large numbers, its mere presence still negatively affects the health of those infected.
Khalili:
They show the sign of the cardio myopathy, aging is faster, neuro-cardiac disorder, the dementia, the renal disease, bone disease. It means that the toxicity associated with the presence of the virus and/or the treatment combination eventually impacts on the health.
LINK:
For Kamel the big problem is the fact that the virus becomes part of the human DNA.
V/O:
So five years ago he started to view HIV in a different light.
Khalili:
We look at HIV/AIDS not as an infectious disease. We look at it as a genetic disease. Because once the viral genome integrate in the host gene in our body, in our DNA, it is a genetic disorder.
LINK:
And by viewing HIV as a genetic disorder opened up new possibilities for treatment.
Khalili:
So how do we deal with a genetic disease? If the gene is mutated, we eliminate the bad gene and if the gene needs to be corrected, we correct the bad gene In this case once HIV is incorporated in our genome, it’s like we now have a bad gene in our chromosomes. So we got to get rid of it. Our approach is get rid of the virus in the cells without hurting the cells.
V/O:
And the way scientists get rid of genes or replace them is through gene editing. A number of these techniques have been developed over the years but one specific technology has taken the world by storm the last few years – CRISPR Cas9.
Michael Pepper:
The CRISPR-Cas9 is now being adapted to edit the genome of for example humans, but all species can be edited.
V/O:
The acronym CRISPR stands for Clustered regularly interspaced short palindro/mic repeats and is a collection of short DNA sequences that have been combined with an enzyme called Cas9.

This combination can then be introduced into a cell. The DNA sequences of CRISPR can be programmed to precisely locate any specific area on the DNA strand. When the area has been located, the Cas9 enzyme cuts through the DNA.
Devi:
Would it be correct if I say that CRISPR-Cas9 technology is like scissors for DNA?
Pepper:
It is more than scissors. So its cuts, but it also replaces the bit that it cuts. And in repairing the DNA you can rewrite the genetic code.
Devi:
How does it know where to cut?
Pepper:
You tell it where to cut. You give it specific guides.
V/O:
The fact that the system can cut out undesired pieces of DNA attracted Kamel’s attention. They found that CRIPR-Cas9 could be used to cut the HIV DNA from human immune cells in the lab.
Khalili:
And then you see there is no evidence for replication of the virus in the cells. And you can identify that this was the area where the virus was integrated and right now there is no virus.
V/O:
They also found that the cell function of the repaired immune cells returned to normal. And when these cells replicate, the new generation of cells were also completely virus free. It also has another advantage.
Khalili:
So we did experiments. We took the eradicated cells, virus free cells, after the treatment and try to infect it with a new virus, re-infection. And we realised that as long as we have the CAS9 and the guide RNA in the cells, that cells remain protected against virus infection.
V/O:
Then they tested the technology on mice. They inserted the CRISPR-Cas9 into hundreds of millions of harmless viruses and programmed them to seek out immune cells infected with HIV.

They then injected millions of these viruses into the blood of the mice.

As the viruses spread through the body, they located infected cells and docked onto them. They then injected the CRISPR-Cas9 into the infected cells. The technology worked its magic – the HIV DNA was cut from the hundreds of millions of infected cells and the mice became HIV free.

It worked time and again. The next step now is human trials.
LINK:
However, some criticism has been raised saying that the technology is not fail-safe and the virus DNA can mutate so CRISPR becomes ineffective.
V/O:
Kamel agrees that mutations can happen if the DNA is cut only in one place where the virus DNA is situated.
Kahlili:
But that is not the strategy we use. We knew that was going to happen. Our strategy is excision. When you clip here and here, you get a chunk of the viral DNA out. There no way for mutation. The virus is dead.
V/O:
And if the virus DNA is removed from immune cells, HIV is cured. Kamel is convinced that this technology could within five or six years spell the end of HIV.
Khalili:
To me it’s like a, I don’t want to call it a magic bullet, but a magic technique.

Michael Pepper: And that DNA is then integrated into the host DNA. So the host DNA carries the virus in the form of DNA in that cell that has now been infected. V/O: The HI virus mainly infects cells associated with the human immune system such as T-cells. Devi: So, HIV is imprinted then in your DNA? Pepper: It constitutes part of your DNA, yes, absolutely. Khalili: And then the cell becomes a factory for the viral production continuously making HIV and budding out from the cells and take the neighbouring cells and that’s the way that basically infection goes on. V/O: As the infection builds, the body’s immune system becomes compromised and people become vulnerable to lethal infections and cancers. LINK: The disease is kept under control by the use of ARV’s or anti-retroviral drugs. V/O: But Kamel says this is not the ultimate solution. Khalili: The current anti-retroviral therapy, which is a useful treatment of AIDS does not eliminate the virus. What is does is inhibits, suppresses replication of the virus. V/O: But even if the virus is not multiplying in large numbers, its mere presence still negatively affects the health of those infected. Khalili: They show the sign of the cardio myopathy, aging is faster, neuro-cardiac disorder, the dementia, the renal disease, bone disease. It means that the toxicity associated with the presence of the virus and/or the treatment combination eventually impacts on the health. LINK: For Kamel the big problem is the fact that the virus becomes part of the human DNA. V/O: So five years ago he started to view HIV in a different light. Khalili: We look at HIV/AIDS not as an infectious disease. We look at it as a genetic disease. Because once the viral genome integrate in the host gene in our body, in our DNA, it is a genetic disorder. LINK: And by viewing HIV as a genetic disorder opened up new possibilities for treatment. Khalili: So how do we deal with a genetic disease? If the gene is mutated, we eliminate the bad gene and if the gene needs to be corrected, we correct the bad gene In this case once HIV is incorporated in our genome, it’s like we now have a bad gene in our chromosomes. So we got to get rid of it. Our approach is get rid of the virus in the cells without hurting the cells. V/O: And the way scientists get rid of genes or replace them is through gene editing. A number of these techniques have been developed over the years but one specific technology has taken the world by storm the last few years – CRISPR Cas9. Michael Pepper: The CRISPR-Cas9 is now being adapted to edit the genome of for example humans, but all species can be edited. V/O: The acronym CRISPR stands for Clustered regularly interspaced short palindro/mic repeats and is a collection of short DNA sequences that have been combined with an enzyme called Cas9. This combination can then be introduced into a cell. The DNA sequences of CRISPR can be programmed to precisely locate any specific area on the DNA strand. When the area has been located, the Cas9 enzyme cuts through the DNA. Devi: Would it be correct if I say that CRISPR-Cas9 technology is like scissors for DNA? Pepper: It is more than scissors. So its cuts, but it also replaces the bit that it cuts. And in repairing the DNA you can rewrite the genetic code. Devi: How does it know where to cut? Pepper: You tell it where to cut. You give it specific guides. V/O: The fact that the system can cut out undesired pieces of DNA attracted Kamel’s attention. They found that CRIPR-Cas9 could be used to cut the HIV DNA from human immune cells in the lab. Khalili: And then you see there is no evidence for replication of the virus in the cells. And you can identify that this was the area where the virus was integrated and right now there is no virus. V/O: They also found that the cell function of the repaired immune cells returned to normal. And when these cells replicate, the new generation of cells were also completely virus free. It also has another advantage. Khalili: So we did experiments. We took the eradicated cells, virus free cells, after the treatment and try to infect it with a new virus, re-infection. And we realised that as long as we have the CAS9 and the guide RNA in the cells, that cells remain protected against virus infection. V/O: Then they tested the technology on mice. They inserted the CRISPR-Cas9 into hundreds of millions of harmless viruses and programmed them to seek out immune cells infected with HIV. They then injected millions of these viruses into the blood of the mice. As the viruses spread through the body, they located infected cells and docked onto them. They then injected the CRISPR-Cas9 into the infected cells. The technology worked its magic – the HIV DNA was cut from the hundreds of millions of infected cells and the mice became HIV free. It worked time and again. The next step now is human trials. LINK: However, some criticism has been raised saying that the technology is not fail-safe and the virus DNA can mutate so CRISPR becomes ineffective. V/O: Kamel agrees that mutations can happen if the DNA is cut only in one place where the virus DNA is situated. Kahlili: But that is not the strategy we use. We knew that was going to happen. Our strategy is excision. When you clip here and here, you get a chunk of the viral DNA out. There no way for mutation. The virus is dead. V/O: And if the virus DNA is removed from immune cells, HIV is cured. Kamel is convinced that this technology could within five or six years spell the end of HIV. Khalili: To me it’s like a, I don’t want to call it a magic bullet, but a magic technique.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Gene therapy snips HIV out of infected cells and makes uninfected cells resistant
metadata.Summary: For the first time, researchers have used a gene-editing technique already used to produce cells resistant to HIV infection to target HIV-infected cells. They have managed to remove HIV genes completely from infected cells, as shown by reductions in the cells' overall rate of HIV production. In cells not already infected, the therapy has itself become part of their genome, producing cells that are resistant to infection for a prolonged period.
metadata.Further information: HIV Genes Have Been Cut Out of Live Animals Using CRISPR. This research will make it more possible to one day do the same in humans In a first, scientists led by Kamel Khalili, director of the Comprehensive NeuroAIDS Center at Temple University, report in the journal Gene Therapy that they have for the first time successfully eliminated HIV genes from the genomes of mice and rats infected with the virus. While rodents don’t get infected with HIV in the same way that humans do, Khalili and his team engineered the animals to incorporate specific HIV genes into nearly every cell in their body, from the brain, heart, liver, kidney lungs and spleen to their blood cells. They then created a pair of molecular scissors using a gene editing technique called CRISPR to snip out the viral genes. CRISPR’s power lies in the fact that it’s precise enough to find and cut out just the viral genes, leaving the animals’ own DNA intact. In previous studies, Khalili used CRISPR to snip out HIV from cells taken from HIV positive people and grown in a lab dish. But proving that it works in a living animal is a huge step forward to developing the technique as a possible treatment, or even cure, for HIV-AIDS. In the study, Khalili studied CRISPR’s ability to remove HIV from both mice and rat models, and found that overall, it was successful in cutting out the virus in more than 50% of the cells of each type. Surprisingly, he achieved this with two simple injections of the molecular CRISPR scissors into a vein in the animals’ tails. “It’s very simple,” he says. “If this technology gets into the clinic to treat human patients, it’s not going to be very complicated. You don’t have to bring the patient to the clinic and do a bone marrow transplant or all kinds of complicated technology. You can basically apply this to any setting.” That’s important is this technique eventually becomes a way to treat people infected with HIV, since the bulk of them live in developed countries where health care facilities aren’t always available. Khalili says this is only one step, albeit an important one, toward that goal. He is currently conducting more studies to determine what dose and how often the CRISPR needs to be given, and monitoring for any side effects of the treatment as well. Because the CRISPR molecule targets HIV genes, it’s unlikely that they will have adverse effects on human DNA, but that’s still an unanswered question that doctors and regulators like the Food and Drug Administration will need to know before they allow the strategy to be tested in human patients. Still, if it’s possible to eliminated HIV from people who are infected, that could lead the way toward curing people of the disease. While anti-HIV drugs are very effective in lowering levels of the virus, they still can’t ferret out every last virus hiding, latent, in some cells. Those hidden reservoirs of HIV are the most dangerous — they can reactivate and cause disease years after the initial infection. But if CRISPR can eliminate them, then that would essentially cure people of their infection. “The first step is to permanently inactivate those viruses incorporated in cells,” says Khalili. “If we can do that, and reach that level, then we may be able to functionally cure individuals or have a sterilizing cure.” Researchers from Lewis Katz School of Medicine at Temple University Successfully Excise HIV DNA from Animals POSTED ON MAY 18, 2016 Using gene editing technology, researchers at the Lewis Katz School of Medicine at Temple University have, for the first time, successfully excised a segment of HIV-1 DNA – the virus responsible for AIDS – from the genomes of living animals. The breakthrough, described online this month in the journal Gene Therapy, is a critical step in the development of a potentially curative strategy for HIV infection. “In a proof-of-concept study, we show that our gene editing technology can be effectively delivered to many organs of two small animal models and excise large fragments of viral DNA from the host cell genome,” explained lead investigator on the study, Kamel Khalili, PhD, Laura H. Carnell Professor and Chair of the Department of Neuroscience, Director of the Center for Neurovirology, and Director of the Comprehensive NeuroAIDS Center at the Lewis Katz School of Medicine at Temple University (LKSOM). Current treatment for HIV infection is centered on the use of a combination of antiretroviral drugs. While antiretroviral drug therapy can effectively suppress HIV replication, it has no ability to eliminate HIV-1 from infected cells. Moreover, when antiretroviral therapy is interrupted, HIV replication rebounds, placing patients at risk for developing acquired immune deficiency syndrome, or AIDS. Such latent infections develop because HIV DNA is able to persist in the genomes of CD4+ memory T-cells and perhaps in other cellular reservoirs where the virus remains silent and is unaffected by current therapy. In earlier research, Dr. Khalili and colleagues were able to show that their novel gene editing system, which is based on CRISPR/Cas9 technology, has the extraordinary ability to eliminate HIV-1 from infected cells in vitro with no adverse effect on the host cells. In ex vivo experiments using clinical specimens, including T-cells from patients infected with HIV that were expanded in culture, they showed that viral replication was significantly reduced following treatment with the gene editing system. The latest study was designed specifically to test whether the gene editing technology could also eliminate HIV-1 in transgenic rats and mice, in which HIV DNA is incorporated into the genome of every cell and organ of the experimental animals. In order to deliver the technology to cells in living animals, Dr. Khalili and colleagues employed a recombinant adeno-associated viral (rAAV) vector delivery system. They also engineered the gene editing apparatus to cleave the integrated HIV-1 DNA in the host cell genome, leading to excision of the viral DNA fragment from the host genome. Two weeks after delivery of the rAAV CRISPR/Cas-9 molecules into the bloodstream, the researchers analyzed the DNA of tissues collected from the animals. The results showed that the targeted segment of HIV-1 DNA had been excised from the viral genome in every tissue, including the brain, heart, kidney, liver, lungs, spleen, and blood cells. Analyses of viral RNA in the rat model showed that the strategy significantly reduced levels of HIV-1 RNA in circulating lymphocytes, as well as in lymph nodes, indicating that viral genome excision had significantly impacted HIV-1 gene expression in cells carrying integrated viral DNA. “The ability of the rAAV delivery system to enter many organs containing the HIV-1 genome and edit the viral DNA is an important indication that this strategy can also overcome viral reactivation from latently infected cells and potentially serve as a curative approach for patients with HIV,” said Dr. Khalili. The excision strategy used in this study, which led to the removal of a large fragment of HIV-1 DNA, eliminates any chance for the development of replication-competent virus or escape events. The clinical implications of the new study are far-reaching. The gene editing platform by itself may be able to eradicate HIV-1 DNA from patients, but it is also highly flexible and potentially could be used in combination with existing antiretroviral drugs to further suppress viral RNA. It also could be adapted to target mutated strains of HIV-1. Dr. Khalili noted that a clinical trial could happen within the next several years. In the meantime, the next step is to conduct a follow-up study in a larger group of animals, in which the researchers plan to monitor for effects of the treatment, its safety, and other important indices. Other researchers contributing to the study include Rafal Kaminski, Chaoran Yin, Jessica Otte, Jennifer Gordon, and Wenhui Hu, Department of Neuroscience, Center for Neurovirology, Lewis Katz School of Medicine at Temple University; Ramona Bella and Pasquale Ferrante, Microbiology and Clinical Microbiology, Department of Biomedical, Surgical and Dental Sciences, University of Milan, Milan, Italy; Howard E. Gendelman, Department of Pharmacology and Experimental Neuroscience, University of Nebraska Medical Center; and Hailong Li and Rosemarie Booze, Behavioral Neuroscience, Department of Psychology, University of South Carolina. The research was supported in part by grants provided by the National Institutes of Health (P30MH092177 and R01NS087971). Editor’s Note: Drs. Khalili, Hu, and Kaminski are named inventors on patents that cover the viral gene editing technology that is the subject of this published journal article. In addition to the foregoing interests, Kamel Khalili, is a co-founder, board member, scientific advisor, and holds equity in Excision Biotherapeutics, a biotech start-up which has licensed the viral gene editing technology from Temple University for commercial development and clinical trials. Jennifer Gordon serves as an unpaid scientific advisor to Excision Biotherapeutics. The option to license the viral gene editing technology was signed prior to the acceptance of this manuscript. The authors declare that this work was produced solely by the authors and that no other individuals or entities influenced any aspects of the work including, but not limited to, the study conception and design; data acquisition, analysis and interpretation; and writing of the manuscript. The work was funded by the National Institutes of Health. No other entities provided funds for the work. The authors further declare that they have received no financial compensation from any other third parties for any aspects of the published work.
